source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: Defines Take The Best (TTB): use recognition first, then look up cues in order of validity, stop at the first cue that discriminates, choose the option it favours. No weighting, no adding up.
numbers: Task: which of two German cities (83 with >100,000 people) is larger; 9 binary cues plus recognition. Cue validity = share of pairs where the cue points the right way (soccer-team cue: 87%).
quote: Search rule: look through cues in order of validity. Stopping rule: stop at first discriminating cue.
limits: One-reason stopping needs a validity order known in advance. The paper is a simulation on one environment, not human data.
agent_relevance: Template for a direct-mode rule: ordered checks, stop at the first decisive one. Fits the S0 class record if checks are ordered by past hit rate.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: Competition: TTB matched the best integrating rule (weighted tallying) and was level with multiple regression on average accuracy, while looking up far fewer cues, under limited knowledge.
numbers: Table 2, mean proportion correct averaged over recognition levels and cue knowledge 10-100%: TTB .658, weighted tallying .658, regression .657, tallying .656, Minimalist .647, Take The Last .645, weighted linear .623, unit-weight linear .621. At 100% cue knowledge: TTB .691, regression .694. 500 simulated individuals in each of 6x84 knowledge types.
limits: Differences among the top four are 0.1-0.2 points: parity, not victory. Regression was fitted on half the objects and tested on the other half, a design later criticised.
agent_relevance: A cheap rule can cost almost nothing in accuracy. Claim 'no loss', not 'gain'.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: Frugality: TTB looks up few cue values; the two simpler variants look up even fewer. Integration rules always look up every cue.
numbers: Average cue values looked up: Take The Last 5.29, Minimalist 5.64, TTB 5.91; TTB range 2 to 20 possible. At half the cities recognised and 50% of cue values known: about 6 lookups.
limits: Counts memory lookups only, not the cost of learning the validity order.
agent_relevance: The saving is search cost. For an agent, count checks or tokens, not memory lookups.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: Even random or lazy cue orderings do well: Minimalist (random order) and Take The Last (last discriminating cue first) lose about one point to TTB.
numbers: Minimalist .647 and Take The Last .645 vs TTB .658. Minimalist rises from .619 (10% cues known) to .674 (100%).
limits: Works because cues in this environment are positively correlated (redundant), so random cues tend to point the same way.
agent_relevance: Cue order matters less in redundant environments. Redundancy is a measurable class feature for S0.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: The recognition principle explains why the weighted and unit-weight linear models did worse (about .62): they let negative cue values outvote recognition. Imposing the principle on them removed the whole gap.
numbers: Unit-weight .621, weighted linear .623 vs TTB .658; gap vanished when recognition principle was added.
limits: Specific to inference from memory with recognition validity about .8 in this task.
agent_relevance: How a rule treats missing or lopsided information can matter more than weighting statistics.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (1996) Reasoning the fast and frugal way: models of bounded rationality
finding: Authors tie TTB to overconfidence and the hard-easy effect: probabilistic mental models predict when these appear, vanish or invert, without confirmation bias.
numbers: Goldstein & Gigerenzer (1996, cited): recognition principle predicted individual choices in about 90% to 100% of cases.
limits: The 90-100% adherence is from early studies; later work found lower adherence when cues contradict recognition (see a13).
agent_relevance: Some 'biases' may be artefacts of how tasks sample the environment. Link to the heuristics-and-biases subfield.

source: Gigerenzer (2012) Homo heuristicus: less-is-more effects in adaptive cognition (Malays J Med Sci review)
finding: Czerlinski, Gigerenzer & Goldstein ran 20 paired-comparison data sets with cross-validation for both models. Tallying beat multiple regression out of sample; regression won only in fitting known data.
numbers: 20 studies (psychological, biological, sociological, economic; 10 from a regression textbook). Cues looked up: TTB 2.4 on average, regression and tallying 7.7. TTB at least as accurate as regression on average.
limits: Fit-versus-prediction crossover. The review itself says the real question is in which environments, not whether.
agent_relevance: Judge a rule on held-out items, not on items it was fitted to (matches G3).

source: Gigerenzer (2012) Homo heuristicus: less-is-more effects in adaptive cognition (Malays J Med Sci review)
finding: Chater, Oaksford, Nakisa & Redington (2003) pitted TTB against a neural net, nearest neighbour, GCM and C4.5 on city size. TTB won or matched at small to moderate training sizes (up to 40% of objects). Brighton's re-analysis with cross-validation showed TTB ahead over the whole range.
numbers: City-population task; training sizes 0-100% of objects.
limits: The original method fitted then tested on the whole sample, which flattered overfitting models; the verdict flipped after the method was corrected.
agent_relevance: Another case where the evaluation method changed the verdict. Supports G3.

source: Gigerenzer (2012) Homo heuristicus: less-is-more effects in adaptive cognition (Malays J Med Sci review)
finding: Why simple rules win: bias-variance decomposition. Total error = bias squared + variance + noise. With sparse or noisy data variance dominates, so a biased but stable rule can beat an unbiased flexible one.
numbers: TTB ordered by plain validity ignores cue dependencies. Ordering by conditional validity (costlier) dropped TTB to the level of the complex models. Cue correlations in the example range from -0.25 to 0.54.
limits: A general statistical fact; the gain shrinks and reverses as data grow.
agent_relevance: Three class features for S0: few examples, noisy outcomes, redundant cues. If they hold, prefer direct or short mode.

source: Gigerenzer (2012) Homo heuristicus: less-is-more effects in adaptive cognition (Malays J Med Sci review)
finding: Field cases of simple beating complex: the hiatus rule (customer inactive after 9 months without purchase) beat the Pareto/NBD model; a one-reason search heuristic beat a Bayesian model and PsycINFO ordering; 1/N beat 14 optimising portfolio models.
numbers: 1/N study: 14 models, 7 investment problems, 10-year estimation window moved month by month. 1/N ranked 1st of 15 on certainty-equivalent return, 2nd on turnover, 5th on Sharpe ratio.
limits: Review written by the programme's founder. The underlying papers were not all opened. 1/N ranking is one analysis.
agent_relevance: Direct rules win in noisy, small-sample domains. Test whether our task classes share that shape.

source: Gigerenzer (2012) Homo heuristicus: less-is-more effects in adaptive cognition (Malays J Med Sci review)
finding: Adaptive toolbox: ten heuristics (recognition, fluency, take-the-best, tallying, satisficing, 1/N, and others) each ecologically rational under stated conditions. Choice among them is shaped by memory state and task structure.
numbers: Recognition heuristic works if recognition validity > 0.5; fluency heuristic if fluency validity > 0.5. Wimbledon 2003 and 2005: recognition predicted matches at equal or higher accuracy than ATP rankings and expert seedings.
limits: The selection mechanism is only partly specified ('mostly unconscious').
agent_relevance: The toolbox maps onto our operators; the open part is exactly the S0 selector.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a decade of research
finding: Origin of the recognition heuristic (RH): a serendipitous result. German students scored slightly higher on American cities than on German cities they knew better.
numbers: Goldstein 1997 dissertation: about 60% of Americans vs 90% of Germans correct on Detroit vs Milwaukee. BBC informal replication: 65% of New York listeners vs 82% of London listeners correct.
limits: Informal, uncontrolled BBC study. Key condition named by the authors: high recognition validity and a representative sample of objects.
agent_relevance: Knowing less wins only when ignorance is informative. Do not drop information blindly.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a decade of research
finding: Boundary conditions: reliance on RH falls when recognition validity is low or when contradicting cues are shown. People do not use it blindly. Authors state no model predicts 96% adherence in all situations.
numbers: Accordance with RH versus recognition validity across experiments: best-fit line r = .57. Oppenheimer (2003, Exp. 2): fictional-city vs real-city pairs gave low accordance. Amateur tennis players predicted the recognised player in about 90% of cases.
limits: Tests adding cues that contradict recognition find many compensatory responses (Newell & Shanks 2004; Hilbig & Pohl 2009). RH is claimed only for memory-based inference.
agent_relevance: A shortcut needs a validity check first. In code: use it only if its past hit rate on this class is above a threshold.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a decade of research
finding: Definition of noncompensatory: a strategy is noncompensatory if each cue weight exceeds the sum of all lower weights, e.g. 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16. Higher cue redundancy favours noncompensatory processing; higher independence favours compensatory.
numbers: Formal definition after Martignon & Hoffrage. Three listed misunderstandings: not universal use; noncompensatory does not mean ignoring all information; model of memory-based inference only.
limits: Stated by the founders in reply to critics.
agent_relevance: A concrete class feature for S0: cue-weight dominance and redundancy.

source: Katsikopoulos (2010) The less-is-more effect: predictions and tests
finding: Formal model of the less-is-more effect with imperfect recognition memory. The effect is predicted to be frequent but small. A new below-chance version is also predicted.
numbers: Simulation with recognition-memory parameters: average magnitude of both effect types about .01 to .02 in accuracy. Almost 50% of prevalence values skewed.
limits: The paper also says current empirical tests have methodological problems. The original condition (Goldstein & Gigerenzer 2002) assumes perfect memory.
agent_relevance: Gains from 'knowing less' are predicted to be one or two points. Do not expect large wins from discarding information.

source: Beaman, Smith, Frosch & McCloy (2010) Less-is-more effects without the recognition heuristic
finding: Less-is-more effects also occur when inference is knowledge-based with limited item knowledge, not only recognition-based. The effect depends on recognition and knowledge validities, which themselves change with the number of items recognised.
numbers: Cites support (Goldstein & Gigerenzer 2002; Frosch et al. 2007; Reimer & Katsikopoulos 2004) and failures to observe it (Boyd 2001; Dougherty et al. 2008; Pohl 2006).
limits: Seeing the effect does not prove recognition-based inference: it follows mathematically from the assumptions.
agent_relevance: Do not read a less-is-more result as proof of a particular mechanism.

source: Schmitt & Martignon (2006) On the accuracy of bounded rationality: how far from optimal is fast and frugal?
finding: Finding the best cue order for a lexicographic rule is hard: no efficient algorithm can approximate the optimum within any constant factor unless P=NP. A simple greedy ordering is proven to perform better than TTB's validity ordering.
numbers: Complexity result plus tight performance-ratio bound for the greedy algorithm.
limits: Worst-case theory. On real data validity ordering is usually near the best (see a19).
agent_relevance: Use cheap orderings; do not search all orders.

source: Simsek & Buckmann (2015) Learning from small samples: an analysis of simple decision heuristics
finding: On 63 natural data sets with a 50/50 train-test split, simple heuristics are close to logistic regression and learn quickly from few examples. Tallying leads early in the learning curve.
numbers: Mean accuracy: logistic regression .747, CART .746, greedy lexicographic .743, take-the-best .743, single-cue .734, tallying .725. Single-cue is 0.9 points behind TTB and 1.3 behind regression. After one training instance expected accuracy is at least 83% of the maximum reachable.
limits: TTB does not beat regression on average here; the earlier 'beats regression' result is not general. Gap about 0.4 points.
agent_relevance: Honest summary for S0: simple rules cost 0.4 to 2 points and need very little data.

source: Simsek & Buckmann (2015) Learning from small samples
finding: Fitting accuracy of cue orderings is nearly the same: best, greedy and validity orders within about 1.6 points; greedy equalled the best order on nearly all data sets.
numbers: Fitting accuracy .758 (best), .756 (greedy), .742 (validity), random lower; 63 data sets.
limits: Validity ordering lost most with continuous or dichotomised cues.
agent_relevance: Order checks by observed accuracy; greedy ordering is cheap.

source: Dawes (1979) The robust beauty of improper linear models; as cited in Gigerenzer review
finding: Equal-weight (improper) linear models predict as well as fitted weights out of sample. Cited second-hand only.
numbers: See a07 for the 20-study cross-validated replay.
limits: Not opened; known only via the review.
agent_relevance: Equal weights are a safe default combiner.

source: DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal (2009) Optimal versus naive diversification: how inefficient is the 1/N portfolio strategy?
finding: None of 14 optimising models consistently beat 1/N on Sharpe ratio, certainty-equivalent return or turnover across 7 data sets. Estimation error cancels the gain from optimising.
numbers: Estimation window needed for sample mean-variance to beat 1/N: about 3000 months for 25 assets, about 6000 months for 50 assets (from the abstract via a search summary).
limits: Not opened: abstract-level only.
agent_relevance: A numeric picture of how much data an optimiser needs; sparse data favours heuristics.

source: Martignon & Hoffrage (2002) Fast, frugal, and fit; with Katsikopoulos & Martignon (2006)
finding: With dependent cues TTB tends to beat tallying, yet tallying or Minimalist can beat TTB. Under conditional independence both can be optimal.
numbers: Qualitative; from search summaries.
limits: Not opened. Treat as a lead.
agent_relevance: The environment, not the rule, decides; measure it.

source: Gigerenzer, Todd & ABC group (1999) Simple heuristics that make us smart; Gigerenzer & Selten (2001) Bounded rationality: the adaptive toolbox
finding: Founding books: the adaptive toolbox is a set of fast and frugal heuristics built from search, stopping and decision rules; Selten's aspiration adaptation supplies the satisficing base. Ecological rationality asks where a rule works, not whether it is rational in general.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Not opened. Critics (Shanks & Lagnado, from a search summary) argue the empirical basis for TTB use by people is weak.
agent_relevance: Citation anchor only.

source: Bogdan (2026) Free energy heuristics: fast-and-frugal cognition as active inference under uncertain precision
finding: Pre-registered LLM test: longer chain of thought hurts on high-meta-uncertainty (Knightian) items but not on definite-answer controls.
numbers: 7 models (5 open-weight 3B-32B, 2 frontier), 5 CoT-length conditions, 7,875 responses, FEH-79 benchmark. Posterior-median accuracy drop on high-regime items 17.3 points (95% credible interval 7.7 to 25.5). Decisive in mid-to-large models, directional in the two frontier models, absent or reversed in the two weakest.
limits: Single-author preprint, not peer reviewed. Items are forecasts and dilemmas, not our task classes. Frontier effect only directional. A Monte Carlo test linking the model to ambiguity-averse policies found no robust correspondence.
agent_relevance: First LLM test of a fast-and-frugal prediction. Supports G1: extra reasoning is not free where evidence precision is uncertain. Test on our items first.

source: Bogdan (2026) Free energy heuristics
finding: Theory: truncating cue use after k cues is optimal when the precision prior has heavy tails. With descending dominance it matches TTB sample for sample; with uniform validity it matches tallying.
numbers: Theorems 2.6.1 and 2.7.x. Recognition heuristic, satisficing and fast-and-frugal trees are only conjectured.
limits: Proven only for TTB and tallying; unreviewed.
agent_relevance: A formal bridge between heuristics and Bayesian control; treat as a hypothesis.

source: Lin, Hou, Li & Yamada (2026) Why linear models can still work in a complex and changing world
finding: Simple linear models can beat flexible ones in a new environment when the nonlinear part is unstable across environments. Stable nonlinear structure favours flexible models; linear models stay vulnerable to linear spurious links.
numbers: Proposition 1 gives a squared-error case where a nonlinear rule learned in training raises target error. No empirical numbers in the abstract.
limits: Preprint, theoretical.
agent_relevance: Choose complexity by stability across environments, not training accuracy: a test for when direct mode generalises.

source: Wikipedia: Take-the-best heuristic (summary of Czerlinski, Goldstein & Gigerenzer 1999)
finding: Secondary summary of the city task with cross-validation: TTB slightly beat regression out of sample.
numbers: 83 German cities, 9 binary cues. Fit: regression 74.3%, TTB 74.2%, unit-weight 74.1%. Generalisation over 10,000 random half-splits: regression 71.9%, TTB 72.2%, unit-weight 71.4%.
limits: Several figures tagged 'citation needed' on the page. Confirm in the 1999 book chapter.
agent_relevance: Gap is 0.3 points: parity.

source: Comparison across a02, a07, a18 and a27
finding: The advantage of the one-reason rule over regression shrinks as more data sets and larger training sets are used.
numbers: City task out of sample +0.3 points (a27); 20-study replay about 0 to small plus (a07); 63 data sets at 50% training -0.4 points (a18).
limits: Different tasks and splits, rough comparison; not a formal meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Plan for parity, not superiority, when setting S0 thresholds.
